question: What was God doing in the 400 years before Jesus was born?
intro: The Old Testament ends with Malachi around 430 BC. The New Testament picks up around 6 BC. In between? Nothing. No prophet, no new scripture, no voice from heaven in Jerusalem. People call it "the silent years." So was God actually silent? And what does that tell you about the quiet stretches in your own life?

days.q: What's the last thing God said, and the first thing He said next?
days.intro: Read the last words of the Old Testament, then the first thing that happens in the New. Four hundred years apart. Pay attention to what Malachi promises and what Zacharias gets told. They're talking about the same thing. Then flip back to Exodus. Israel waited in Egypt for 430 years before God "remembered" them. Same number. Nobody notices that.
days.journal: The angel tells Zacharias "thy prayer is heard." He'd been praying a long time. What have you been praying about long enough that you've started wondering if anyone's listening?

days.q: What was it like to live in the gap?
days.intro: The people in Luke 1 and 2 weren't sitting in a bubble. Persia ran things, then Greece, then Rome. Synagogues, Pharisees, and Sadducees all showed up during this stretch. So did the Greek Old Testament the Apostles quoted from later. Let's look at Simeon and Anna. Everybody seemed to be doing their own thing, but they kept showing up to the temple, waiting for a promise.
days.journal: Simeon and Anna waited in the temple for decades. What do you think kept them coming back?

days.q: Was God silent *everywhere*?
days.intro: Here's where the Restoration flips the question. While Jerusalem heard nothing, God was talking constantly on another continent. Samuel the Lamanite gave the exact sign. Nephi got a direct answer the night before it happened. The "silence" was a Jerusalem problem, not a God problem.
days.journal: They kept watching even with a death date set. What are you still watching for that other people have given up on?

days.q: What do prophets say about waiting on God?
days.intro: Here's what we got: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf gave an awesome talk on this back in 2010. Read it. He tells us what waiting is supposed to look like.

read.speaker: Dieter F. Uchtdorf
read.section: Start at the marshmallow experiment and read through his definition of patience.

days.takeaway: His point is that patience isn't passive. We're supposed to *actively* wait. Do everything we can while the answer is delayed. He said "Patience is not passive resignation, nor is it failing to act because of our fears." He teaches that this is what turns regular people into real disciples.
days.journal: Where in your life are you "waiting" when you should be doing more?

days.q: Why would God go quiet for so long?
days.intro: This is uncomfortable, but let it sit with you. If God loves His children, why would He let 400 years go by without a prophet? It's easy to say "the people rejected Him," but you don't believe there were *zero* good people on the earth, do you? Joseph Smith asked the same thing from a jail cell: "O God, where art thou?" He didn't get scolded for asking. Now, don't answer the question yet. Read the stuff below and let your mind chew on it.
days.journal: Have you had a stretch where God felt silent? Looking back now, was He?

days.q: How do you wait? How *should* you wait?
days.intro:
Waiting sucks sometimes, mostly because we often just sit there. When you do something while waiting, it's not nearly as bad. Same thing with life. Waiting on God is easier when we're actively doing good.

Two stories today: Joseph got thrown in prison for doing the right thing, ran the prison well anyway, was forgotten for two more years by the dude he helped, and was still ready when the call came. Alma's people were in bondage and God didn't free them. They had to stay in bondage and finally God made their burdens light, but they were still waiting to be freed.

When you read, pick out what people are doing while they wait on the Lord.
days.journal: Pick one thing you've been waiting on. What can you do this week that helps you actively wait for it? Don't be a wuss, pick something real and write it down.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Go back to the beginning. Read the angel's words to Zacharias with the whole week behind you.
days.journal: Answer the week's question in three or four sentences: What was God doing in the 400 years before Jesus was born? And what's He doing in the quiet parts of your life?

question: Why did Jesus have to be baptized?
intro: John the Baptist asked this first. He actually tried to talk Jesus out of it. Baptism is for the forgiveness of sins. Jesus had none. So what was the point? The answer says a lot about what baptism really is, and about what you're doing every Sunday when you take the sacrament.

days.q: What actually happened at the Jordan?
days.intro: Four writers, four angles. Read them back to back. Notice what each one includes that the others skip. Notice John's objection and what Jesus says back.
days.journal: Before this week, what would you have said if someone asked why Jesus got baptized? Write it down. We'll check it on Day 7.

days.q: What does "fulfil all righteousness" even mean?
days.intro: Jesus gives John a one-line reason and it's kind of cryptic. Two things help. The Greek word behind "baptize" (baptizo) means to dip or dunk. And "righteousness" here doesn't mean sinless. It means doing what the Father asks. Read what John was doing before Jesus showed up, so you know what baptism meant to the people standing on the riverbank.
read: Luke 3:10-14 (people asking John "what shall we do then?")
days.journal: If "righteousness" means doing what the Father asks, not being flawless, what does that do to the word for you?

days.q: Who answered this 600 years early?
days.intro: Nephi asks this exact question, almost word for word, and then answers it. He's on the other side of the world and six centuries early. Read him first. Then read how the Lord defines baptism in our day.
days.journal: Nephi says Jesus was baptized to show the way. Who's watching you to see the way?

days.q: What do apostles say baptism actually is?
days.intro: Elder Robert D. Hales gave this talk after two years of surgeries kept him out of conference. He came back and spent his whole time on what our baptism commits us to. Read it.

read.talk: The Covenant of Baptism: To Be in the Kingdom and of the Kingdom
read.speaker: Robert D. Hales
read.section: Read the section on what we promise at baptism.

days.takeaway: Baptism is the doorway into God's kingdom, and when you walk through it you're picking a side. He said "At that point we have chosen to be of His kingdom and not of the world." You're not just *in* the kingdom. You're *of* it.
days.journal: Do you think of yourself as "in" the kingdom, "of" the kingdom, or both? What's the difference?

days.q: If Jesus didn't need it, is baptism about need or about following?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. If a sinless person still gets baptized, then baptism can't only be about washing sin away. Fine. But if it's required of *everyone*, what about the billions of people who never got the chance? Little kids? People born 1,000 years before Christ in the middle of nowhere? The Restoration has answers, but don't skip to them. Read these as answers to a real problem.
read: D&C 137:5-10 (Joseph sees his brother Alvin, who died unbaptized)
days.journal: What's the hardest part of "baptism is required" for you? Be honest. Nobody's reading this but you.

days.q: What does a baptized person actually do differently?
days.intro: Alma at the waters of Mormon gives the clearest description in scripture of what the covenant looks like Monday through Saturday. Then the sacrament prayer, which is you standing back in the Jordan every week. Read them together and pick out the promises.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 3, "Baptism, Our First Covenant"
days.journal: Next Sunday, what would it look like to take the sacrament like you were getting baptized again? Pick one thing you'd do differently.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to John's objection and what Jesus told him. Then read what you wrote on Day 1.
days.journal: Answer the week's question in three or four sentences: Why did Jesus have to be baptized? And why did you?

question: Why did Jesus fast for 40 days before doing anything else?
intro: Before a single sermon, miracle, or disciple, Jesus went into the desert alone and didn't eat for 40 days. It's the *first* thing He does after baptism. If fasting matters that much, why does it feel like a chore once a month?

days.q: What actually happened in the wilderness?
days.intro: Read Matthew and Luke. Then read the Joseph Smith Translation change to the first verse. It flips the reason He went out there. And watch how Jesus answers every temptation. Same move, three times.
read: Joseph Smith Translation, Matthew 4:1 (in the footnote)
days.journal: The JST says the Spirit led Him there "to be with God." When was the last time you went somewhere just to be with God? Not to church. Somewhere on purpose.

days.q: Why 40, and why the desert?
days.intro: Forty shows up all over scripture. Moses on the mountain. Israel in the wilderness. Elijah walking to Horeb. It's the number for "long enough to be changed." And here's the part most people miss: every scripture Jesus throws back at Satan comes from one chapter in Deuteronomy about Israel's own 40 years. He was fasting inside a story He already knew.
days.journal: Elijah wanted to die, and the angel's answer was food and sleep. When have you needed rest more than a lesson?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon say fasting actually does?
days.intro: The Book of Mormon treats fasting like a tool, not a checkbox. The sons of Mosiah fasted and became teachers who could actually teach. The priests fasted for Alma the Younger while he lay there unable to move. When you read, look for the results. What did fasting *get* them?
days.journal: Alma 17:3 says they fasted and prayed much and it gave them something specific. What was it? Have you ever fasted for that?

days.q: What do prophets say fasting is for?
days.intro: President Henry B. Eyring, April 2015. He spends the talk on the law of the fast, and specifically on the half we skip: the offering.

read.talk: Is Not This the Fast That I Have Chosen?
read.speaker: Henry B. Eyring
read.section: Read the opening through the Isaiah 58 section.

days.takeaway: Fasting is a commandment simple enough for a kid, with real promises attached. And the offering is what turns your hunger into somebody else's meal. He called it "a commandment so simple that a child can understand it." Simple isn't the same as small.
days.journal: When's the last time you fasted for something specific *and* gave a real offering with it? What happened?

days.q: Does skipping food actually do anything?
days.intro: Honest question. Is fasting a spiritual tool, or a ritual we keep because we always have? If you've ever fasted, gotten a headache, and felt nothing else, you've asked this. Isaiah 58 is God answering people who asked the same thing. Read it as a rebuke and a promise, because it's both.
days.journal: Isaiah describes a fast God rejects and a fast He chooses. Which one is closer to your usual fast Sunday? No spin. Just look at it.

days.q: How do you fast with a purpose?
days.intro: A fast with no purpose is just hunger. Every time scripture talks about fasting, it pairs it with prayer and a specific reason. A question, a person, a need. Esther asked everyone to fast for her before she walked in on the king and risked her life. Alma tells us straight how he came to know what he knows. Read them both and figure out what their fasts had that yours usually doesn't.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 4, "The Law of the Fast"
days.journal: If you decided right now, what's the one thing you'd fast for next fast Sunday? Write it down so you can't pretend you forgot.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the desert.
days.journal: Answer the week's question in three or four sentences: Why did Jesus fast before He started? What is fasting actually for?

question: "Be ye therefore perfect." What was Jesus actually asking?
intro: It's the last line of a chapter that's already hard, and it reads like an impossible bar. Most of us hear "perfect," think "flawless," and quietly give up. But that's probably not the word Jesus used. This week is about finding out what He actually meant, and what you're supposed to do about it.

days.q: What does the verse say, and what's around it?
days.intro: Read the whole passage, not just the last line. Jesus is talking about loving your enemies when He says it. That's the context. Then read the same sermon when the resurrected Christ gives it in the Book of Mormon. He changes one word. Find it.
days.journal: What does "perfect" mean to you right now, before this week starts? Write it down so you can compare on Day 7.

days.q: What word did Jesus actually use?
days.intro: The Greek word is *teleios*. It means complete, finished, mature, having reached its purpose. Not flawless. A full-grown oak is teleios compared to an acorn. Read the other places the New Testament uses the same word and watch what happens to the meaning.
days.journal: If Jesus had said "be ye therefore *complete*," what changes about the ask?

days.q: Who does the completing?
days.intro: The Restoration answers the "how" question head on. Read these and look for who's doing the perfecting in each verse. Spoiler: it's not you.
days.journal: Moroni says "come unto Christ, and be perfected in him." What's your part of that sentence, and what's His?

days.q: What are apostles saying about this right now?
days.intro: Two talks. Elder Jeffrey R. Holland's is the one everybody quotes, and he built it on a word study President Russell M. Nelson did back in 1995. Read Holland's first. If you've got time left, skim Nelson's part on the Greek.

read.speaker: Jeffrey R. Holland
read.section: Read the opening through the Tolstoy story.

days.takeaway:
Holland's point is that the commandment is about your potential, not your report card, and turning it into self-loathing gets it exactly backwards. He said "except for Jesus, there have been no flawless performances on this earthly journey." He calls the other thing toxic perfectionism, and he's not being cute about it.

Nelson's point is that the word means finished or complete, and scripture uses that same word about Jesus Himself reaching it *after* the Resurrection. Perfection is pending. For everyone.
days.journal: Write down one sentence from either talk you want to keep.

days.q: If God does the perfecting, why does Jesus command it?
days.intro: Here's the tension. Day 3 said Christ perfects us. But Matthew 5:48 is a command, and commands mean you're supposed to do something. Both are true. So how? Read the parable Holland uses and pay attention to what the forgiven servant was expected to do afterward. Then read Paul, both halves of the verse.
days.journal: Where in your life are you trying to be finished with something God isn't finished with yet?

days.q: What does steady improvement actually look like?
days.intro: Not a leap. A pace. King Benjamin says it flat out: don't run faster than you have strength. Amulek says now is the time, but the time is for *preparing*, not arriving. When you read, look for the pattern.
read: Preach My Gospel, chapter 6, "Developing Christlike Attributes" intro and the attribute activity
days.journal: Pick one attribute from PMG chapter 6. What's one small thing this week that moves you toward it? Small on purpose. Then actually do it.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the verse. Read it with the whole week behind you, then read what you wrote on Day 1.
days.journal: Rewrite Matthew 5:48 in your own words. Then compare it to what you wrote on Day 1.

question: If God is your Father, why do you talk to Him like a stranger?
intro: Preach My Gospel starts with one sentence: God is our loving Heavenly Father. Not a force. Not a boss. A dad. If that's true, it should change how you pray. But most of us pray the same way we'd write a formal email. This week is about what it actually means that He's your Father, and what to do about it.

days.q: What did Jesus say about how to pray?
days.intro: Jesus taught His disciples to pray exactly once in scripture, and it's short. Read it, then read what He said right before it about people who pray to be seen. When you read, notice what word He uses for God in the very first line.
days.journal: Be honest. How do your prayers usually start, and how long before you get to what you actually want to say?

days.q: What did it mean to call God "Father" back then?
days.intro: Jews in Jesus's day almost never called God "Father" in prayer. It was too familiar. Jesus did it constantly, and then told everyone else to. The word He probably used was *Abba*, the everyday word a kid uses. Paul picked it up later. Read where it shows up and what Paul says it means.
days.journal: If you called God "Dad" in your prayer tonight, would it feel wrong? Why?

days.q: What do we know about Him that others don't?
days.intro: The Restoration gives us specifics. God has a body. He's a real Person. We lived with Him before we came here. Joseph Smith saw Him, and the first thing the Father did was call Joseph by name. Read these looking for what kind of Father He is, not just that He is one.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 1, "God Is Our Loving Heavenly Father"
days.journal: Moses 1 shows God calling Moses "my son" before giving him a single assignment. What would change if you believed He sees you that way first?

days.q: What do prophets say about praying like a son or daughter?
days.intro: Elder David A. Bednar, October 2008. He spends the whole talk on prayer, but the part that matters is what he says about praying with real intent, and about praying *for* people instead of just about them.
days.takeaway: His point is that prayer isn't a performance. You pray with real intent, meaning you're actually going to act on what you ask for. He teaches that our prayers become more meaningful when we pray for others and then go do something about it. The prayer and the doing are one thing.
days.journal: What did you pray for last that you didn't actually do anything about?

days.q: If He's a loving Father, why doesn't He answer?
days.intro: This is the one everybody asks. You pray, nothing. You pray harder, still nothing. If a dad ignored his kid like that we'd call it neglect. Don't defend God here. Read these and let the question sit. Some of them are answers. Some just tell you that His not answering yet isn't the same as not listening.
days.journal: What's the prayer you've stopped praying because it never got answered? Write it down. Then write what you'd do if you found out He'd heard every one.

days.q: How do you actually talk to Him differently?
days.intro: Enos went into the woods and prayed all day and all night. Nobody's asking you to do that. But read how he describes it. It's a conversation. He says something, God says something back, he says something else. When you read, look for what makes a prayer a conversation instead of a speech.
days.journal: Tonight, pray out loud, alone, and talk to Him like He's in the room. Then write one sentence about how it went.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the Lord's Prayer. Read it slowly, then read what you wrote on Day 1.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: If God is your Father, why do you talk to Him like a stranger? And what are you going to do about it?

question: What does "born again" mean, and did Nicodemus ever get it?
intro: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin. Smart, religious, respected. He came to Jesus at night, probably so nobody would see. And Jesus told him he had to be born again. He didn't get it. He asked if he was supposed to climb back into his mother. Most of us nod along at the phrase without understanding it any better than he did.

days.q: What did Jesus actually say to him?
days.intro: Read the whole conversation. Notice that Nicodemus never asks the question Jesus answers. Jesus just starts in. And notice what Jesus says being born again requires. Two things, not one.
days.journal: Nicodemus came at night. What's something about your faith you'd rather ask about in the dark?

days.q: What does "born of water and of the Spirit" mean?
days.intro: The Greek phrase can mean "born again" or "born from above." Both work and Jesus probably meant both. Water is baptism. Spirit is the Holy Ghost. That's the same two steps John the Baptist described. Read the crowd in Acts 2 asking what to do, then Ezekiel's promise of a new heart.
days.journal: The crowd in Acts 2 asked "what shall we do?" When's the last time you asked God that and meant it?

days.q: What does it feel like when it actually happens?
days.intro: The Book of Mormon has the clearest description in scripture. King Benjamin's people hear a sermon and something happens to them. Alma the Younger describes it from the inside. When you read, look for what changed in them. Not what they did. What they *wanted*.
days.journal: Alma asks if you've experienced a mighty change in your heart. Have you? When?

days.q: What do apostles say being born again looks like?
days.intro: Elder D. Todd Christofferson, April 2008. He gave a whole talk with this exact title and he's blunt about the fact that it usually isn't a single moment.

read.speaker: D. Todd Christofferson
read.section: Read the whole thing. It's short.

days.takeaway: His point is that being born again is usually a process, not an event. For most people it happens gradually, through covenants and the Holy Ghost working on you over years. If you're waiting for a lightning bolt before you count yourself born again, you might be waiting for the wrong thing.
days.journal: Do you feel like you're "still being born again" or like it already happened? What's the evidence either way?

days.q: Did Nicodemus ever get it?
days.intro: Here's the part people skip. Nicodemus shows up two more times in John. Read them in order. He defends Jesus, carefully. Then after the crucifixion he shows up with a hundred pounds of burial spices, in daylight, when it was dangerous. Scripture never says he was baptized. So did he get it? Don't answer fast.
days.journal: Nicodemus went from sneaking in at night to carrying spices in daylight. What's your version of that? What would "daylight" look like for you?

days.q: How do you stay born again?
days.intro: Alma asks the question nobody wants to hear: if you felt it once, can you feel it now? Being born again isn't a trophy. It's a direction. When you read, look for what Alma and Paul say you keep doing.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 3, "The Gift of the Holy Ghost"
days.journal: What's one thing you did this week that felt like walking in the Spirit, and one that didn't?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the night conversation. Read the first few verses again with the whole week behind you.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What does "born again" mean? And did it happen to you?

question: Does God call the qualified, or qualify the called?
intro: Jesus picked fishermen. Not scribes, not rabbis, not anyone with a résumé. Peter's first real words to Jesus were "depart from me, I am a sinful man." That's who He built the Church on. So when God asks you to do something you're not ready for, is that a mistake, or is that the point?

days.q: Who did Jesus actually call, and what did they say?
days.intro: Read the calling of the first disciples in Luke. Pay attention to Peter's reaction. It's not "yes." Then read Matthew's version, which is shorter and has one detail Luke leaves out: how fast they went.
days.journal: Peter's first response to Jesus was basically "you've got the wrong guy." When have you felt that way about something God asked of you?

days.q: What did it mean to be a fisherman in Galilee?
days.intro: Not glamorous. Long nights, smelly work, taxed hard by Rome. Fishermen weren't educated in the law. The religious leaders later called Peter and John "unlearned and ignorant." That's the crew Jesus chose. Read what the leaders said, and read what Paul said about who God picks.
read: Judges 6:11-16 (Gideon, hiding from the enemy, called "mighty man of valour")
days.journal: God called Gideon a mighty warrior while he was hiding in a hole. What does God call you that you don't believe yet?

days.q: What does the Restoration say about who gets called?
days.intro: D&C 4 was given to Joseph Smith's dad, a farmer with no church experience. Read what it says qualifies you. Then read Enoch, who told God he was just a kid everybody hated and couldn't talk right. When you read, list the qualifications. They're not what you'd expect.
days.journal: D&C 4 lists what qualifies someone. Which one do you actually have, and which one are you faking?

days.q: What do prophets say about being called before you're ready?
days.intro: President Henry B. Eyring, October 2002. He was asked to give a talk about raising the bar for missionaries and instead gave one about how the Lord makes people equal to their calls.

read.speaker: Henry B. Eyring
read.section: Read the first half, through the story of his own calling.

days.takeaway: His point is that the call comes first and the ability comes after, not the other way around. God doesn't wait until you're qualified. He calls you and then, if you go, He qualifies you as you serve. Waiting to feel ready is how you never go.
days.journal: What are you waiting to feel ready for? What if you're supposed to start before that happens?

days.q: But doesn't God sometimes call people who fail?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Saul was anointed king and lost it. Being called doesn't guarantee anything. So what's the difference between the fisherman who becomes Peter and the one who walks away? Read these and don't make it easy.
read: Alma 39:1-4 (Corianton, a called missionary who blew it)
Alma 39:9-13 (and what Alma told him to do about it)
days.journal: Corianton failed badly and Alma still told him to go back to work. Where have you disqualified yourself when God hasn't?

days.q: How do you get qualified?
days.intro: Same D&C 4 verse from Day 3, but now read it as a to-do list. Then read Moroni, who spent his whole life doing a job he felt unqualified for and said so. When you read, look for what the Lord says He does with weakness.
days.journal: Name one thing God has asked of you where you're waiting to feel qualified. What's the first step you could take anyway? Do it this week.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the boat. Read Peter's reaction one more time.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Does God call the qualified, or qualify the called? And which one are you acting like is true?
